subject: pharmacology
title: Antiarrhythmic drugs

steps.tx: The Vaughan Williams system sorts drugs by dominant channel: class I blocks sodium, class II blocks beta receptors, class III blocks potassium and class IV blocks calcium. **Adenosine**, digoxin and magnesium sit outside the classes as unclassified essentials. Every class can also provoke arrhythmia, which is called **proarrhythmia** and limits casual use. Structural heart disease vetoes several agents outright in examination stems. Monitoring is part of the prescription itself for this whole class.
steps.say: Vaughan Williams is organisational because it sorts drugs by dominant channel blocked in membranes. Sodium and beta and potassium and calcium classes are separate because they organise thinking for prescribers. Every antiarrhythmic is risky because it can also provoke arrhythmia in susceptible patients. Structural heart disease is restrictive because it forbids several agents outright for patient safety.

vis.alt: Vaughan Williams grid: class I sodium blockers procainamide, lidocaine and flecainide; class II beta blockers metoprolol and esmolol; class III potassium blockers amiodarone and sotalol with QT lengthening and torsades risk; class IV calcium blockers verapamil and diltiazem; unclassified adenosine, digoxin and magnesium.
vis.caption: Class is defined by the dominant channel; every class can provoke arrhythmia.

steps.tx: Amiodarone controls dangerous ventricular rhythms and atrial fibrillation when other drugs fail, but its burden grows with time. Its iodine load and tissue stores injure **thyroid**, lung, liver, cornea and skin over months of therapy. Baseline and periodic organ checks are therefore mandatory, not optional extras. It interacts through metabolic pathways and raises **digoxin** levels predictably. Dronedarone is weaker, lacks iodine and is barred in permanent atrial fibrillation with heart failure.
steps.say: Amiodarone controls dangerous rhythms but burdens many organs slowly. Thyroid and lung and liver and eye checks are mandatory. It interacts widely and raises digoxin levels predictably. Scheduled monitoring is part of safe prescribing for amiodarone.

steps.tx: Flecainide suppresses atrial fibrillation well in structurally normal hearts, including pill in the pocket strategies for selected patients. The CAST lesson proved class Ic drugs kill after infarction by provoking ventricular arrhythmia in scarred muscle. **Sotalol** mixes beta and potassium blockade and carries torsades risk needing QT surveillance. **Digoxin** slows nodal conduction vagally for rate control but intoxicates with renal failure and low potassium. Substrate decides safety more than rhythm appearance ever does.
steps.say: Flecainide is restricted because it suits structurally normal hearts only for atrial fibrillation control. After infarction it is dangerous because it provokes ventricular arrhythmia and increases mortality risk. Sotalol is monitored because it risks torsades and needs QT surveillance at regular intervals. Digoxin is narrow because it intoxicates easily when kidneys fail or potassium falls low.

steps.tx: **Adenosine** blocks the atrioventricular node for seconds, ending nodal supraventricular tachycardia and unmasking flutter waves during the pause. Give it as a rapid push and warn about flushing, chest tightness and breathlessness that pass quickly. Unknown wide complex tachycardia is treated as ventricular, and **verapamil** there can collapse the patient catastrophically. Verapamil is also dangerous in Wolff Parkinson White atrial fibrillation with rapid conduction. Procainamide or cardioversion leads when the complex is wide and uncertain.
steps.say: Adenosine is brief because it freezes the nodal pathway for seconds during supraventricular tachycardia. It is diagnostic because it ends tachycardia and reveals flutter waves during the pause. Unknown wide complex tachycardia is ventricular because it is treated as ventricular until proved otherwise. Verapamil is dangerous because it can collapse such patients and is avoided in this setting.

steps.tx: Twisting QRS complexes with prolonged QT mean **torsades de pointes**, treated by stopping culprits and giving intravenous **magnesium** first. Replete potassium and shorten repolarisation with overdrive pacing or isoprenaline when episodes recur. Standard class I agents worsen torsades and must never be used here. Every antiarrhythmic start deserves electrocardiogram, electrolyte, thyroid, kidney and interaction review beforehand. Suppressing appearances in scarred hearts worsens survival, so indications stay deliberately narrow.
steps.say: Twisting complexes with long QT indicate torsades de pointes clearly. Magnesium is first treatment after stopping culprit drugs immediately. Potassium repletion and faster pacing shorten repolarisation safely. Standard sodium blockers worsen torsades and must be avoided.

steps.tx: The tracing shows **prolonged QT**, an **R on T** premature beat and a lower strip of twisting QRS that is **torsades de pointes**, with intravenous magnesium cued in the corner. Reading left to right teaches the sequence examiners love: substrate, trigger, then polymorphic storm. Treatment is magnesium, potassium and faster pacing after stopping culprits, never more class I drug. This image anchors the rule that repolarisation prolongation kills differently from conduction block.
steps.say: The tracing shows prolonged QT and an early beat triggering torsades. Twisting QRS complexes confirm polymorphic ventricular tachycardia clearly. Magnesium treats torsades after culprit drugs are stopped immediately. Potassium and pacing shorten repolarisation when episodes recur frequently.
